get.summary: List config change history.
get.description:
**No restore endpoint, and deliberately so** (RFC 0004-bis A5, declined —
see the RFC's decision log for the recorded row).

`config_changes` stores a *diff summary* — added, removed and changed
registry names — and never the config itself. `POST …/history/{id}/restore`
cannot be built on that: a list of registry names does not reconstruct a
TOML file. Making it possible means storing the full config content per
change, and `config.toml` carries `upstream_auth` credentials, static bearer
tokens and OIDC client secrets. That would put every secret this instance
has ever been configured with into a table any admin can read through an
API, retained indefinitely and surviving the rotation that was supposed to
end their life.

The revert path that exists is the config editor: it shows the live content,
accepts a replacement, and validates before staging. What it lacks is the
*previous* content to paste, and closing that honestly is a question about
where config history should live — a git-backed config, or an encrypted
store — not a field on this response.

**The coordinates are spent, not freed** (RFC 0016 §4.4). Each version is
tombstoned: the bytes, the README and the listing entry go, and the version
number can never be published again. This is the only local-registry delete
path in the API, so it is also the only place a coordinate is ever burned.

Unlike the sibling bulk handlers this does not reach into `backend` directly.
A delete is four coordinated effects — tombstone, bytes, README, cache — and
they belong together in `LocalRegistryService::delete_version`, next to the
ordering constraint that makes them safe to interrupt.

row in two steps, and a blob caught in that window has its row by the next
sweep. So the first run on a fresh estate deletes nothing and reports
`first_seen_orphaned` — run it again to collect them.

`dry_run` reports without deleting **and without advancing anything toward
deletion**: previewing twice is not the same as running twice.

Run retention over a local/hybrid registry's published versions (admin).
post.description:
**A version survives if *any* configured keep condition matches.** There is
no expression to write and no ordering to get wrong: the only way to reclaim
a version is for every configured condition to decline to keep it. Wrong
configuration therefore fails toward keeping.

A reclaimed version leaves a tombstone and its number can never be taken
again. Freeing disk must not free the *namespace*, or retention becomes a
supply-chain mechanism by accident (RFC 0016 §4.2).

`409` when the registry has no `[registries.retention]` block, or one with no
keep condition. Not a silent no-op: an operator calling this believes they
are reclaiming space, and a `200 {"reclaimed": 0}` would confirm it.

parameters.name: dry_run
parameters.description:
Report without reclaiming. Absent falls back to the registry's configured
`dry_run`, which itself defaults to `true`.

A caller may pass `true` to preview against a registry configured live,
but passing `false` does **not** override a configured `dry_run = true`:
an operator who armed the safety catch should not have it taken off by a
query string.

post.summary: Pin a version against retention, or release the pin (admin).
post.description:
A pinned version is never reclaimed by a retention run, whatever the
registry's policy says — the escape every automatic policy needs, for the
release an LTS customer runs and the pull statistics will eventually stop
defending (RFC 0016 §4.1).

It is a **keep, never a reclaim**. There is deliberately no spelling of this
endpoint that makes retention *more* aggressive for one version, because a
policy that deletes should not be reachable one version at a time.

Pinning changes nothing else: the version resolves, downloads and lists
exactly as it did. Pinning a coordinate that is already deleted is a no-op —
a spent coordinate cannot be protected from a reclamation that can never
reach it.

code for tokens, and redirect the browser to the SPA with the tokens in the

The returned `state` must match an entry this server created and has not yet
consumed, or nothing is exchanged. The caller then compares the echoed

get.summary: Redirect the browser to the OIDC provider's authorization endpoint.
get.description:
The caller supplies a `state` query parameter holding a random value it has
kept locally (`sessionStorage` in the SPA, memory in the CLI). That value is
**not** what goes to the identity provider: the server generates its own
unguessable handle, records the caller's value against it along with the PKCE
verifier and nonce, and sends only the handle. The caller's value comes back
at the end of the flow so it can confirm this callback belongs to the login
it started.

The two halves protect different things and neither replaces the other. The
server-side entry gives PKCE verifier custody, one-time redemption, expiry
and provider binding; the caller's value is what ties the flow to a
particular browser or CLI process, which the server cannot observe.

Omitting `state` (e.g. a HEAD probe) returns 200 when OIDC is configured,
503 when it is not — useful for the frontend to decide whether to show the
"Sign in with OIDC" button.

get.description:
The `sumdb/` half of the `GOPROXY` protocol, and until this route existed it
was simply absent: `go mod download` through BatleHub still opened a direct
connection to `sum.golang.org` for every module it had not seen. So the
proxy had *moved* the egress rather than removed it, and an air-gapped
estate failed closed on a lookup it could not make.

`sum.golang.org` is reachable buys nothing; cached, the second build needs no
route off the site. Caching is sound because the log is signed — the
signature travels with the bytes, so a cached checksum record is exactly as
trustworthy as a live one, and this proxy neither parses nor rewrites it.

a transparency log the client rejects.

Optional, and its absence is reported rather than assumed: a simulation
with no address cannot answer for the IP block layer, and answering
"allow" because none was supplied is the same defect this endpoint had
one level down (RFC 0004-bis B4). See `covers` on the response.

The permission to simulate, e.g. `releases:read`.

Parsed into [`Action`] rather than compared as a string. Before RFC 0015
phase 1 an unknown value here was answered rather than refused: the rule
chain compared it to the config's strings, nothing matched, and the
simulator returned **deny** with a rule name attached — a confident
answer about a permission that does not exist. The page whose whole
purpose is "would this identity be allowed" is the worst possible place
for a typo to look like a policy decision.

AdvisoryRelation.description:
Why a coordinate is in the caller's list.

The two are different relationships and are labelled rather than merged: you
are *exposed to* what you pulled, and you can *fix* what you own (RFC 0004
R7). The same coordinate can be both, in which case it appears once under
`owned` — the actionable relationship wins. A version you pulled and a
different version you own are two coordinates and stay two rows (R15).

package archive or signature — streamed from cache storage or from the
configured upstream.

The `Content-Type` is the one the registry protocol calls for; the payload is
never parsed by this server on the read path.

reads it the same way when selecting builds.

Every field is what the *tiers* composed to, not what a particular version
row holds: a per-package `visibility` override lives in the `policy` table
and is composed in here, while the legacy per-package visibility on the
package row is one of the layers `not_covered` names.

Empty for almost every coordinate. Present here because an `allow` on a
version whose `cve_gate` is exempt is a materially different answer from
an `allow` on one that passed it.

declared its own.

verdict of the registry. Ignored by `backfill`.

tells two signers apart; it is the public half and not a secret.

written again.

writes them again under their key — the store dedups by content, so
the count is of keys, not of bytes moved.

not a storage key, a registry this instance does not have.

asking for one they do not is `403`, not a silent drop.

before this field carried. "All of mine" is a client-side convenience
(`batlehub auth token create --all-groups`) that sends the resolved list
here, not a second server-side spelling of the same thing.

Accepts "user" or "admin" (admin callers only for "admin").

the only moment it can be changed — a snapshot is fixed for the life of
the token, so a wrong one is re-created, never edited.

e.g. `"idea/idea-2026.1.3.tar.gz"`. Takes precedence over name+version.

artifact_key.description: The logical storage key that was targeted.

deleted.description: `true` if the artifact was present and removed; `false` if it was not cached.

removed.description:
Whether a row was actually there. `false` is a success: removal is
idempotent, and an operator who ran it twice deserves to know which.

message.description:
Optional human-readable deprecation message (mirrored into npm's native
`deprecated` field for npm registries).

evicted_keys.description: The storage keys evicted, or that would be under `dry_run`.

incomplete_because.description:
Set when the run stopped before answering the whole question — a
`dry_run` size-cap preview that ran out of page while the registry was
still over the cap.

keys_truncated.description:
How many keys were dropped from `evicted_keys`. Non-zero means the list
is a sample, not the answer.

ExemptionDto.description: The exemption as it is read back, carrying the self-approval marker.

self_approved.description:
Set when the principal that granted the exemption also published the
version. **A marker, not a refusal** — see [`GateExemption`].

ExemptionListEntry.description: One live exemption, with everything the panel filters on.

expired.description:
Already past. Listed anyway: an expired exemption silences nothing, and a
page whose subject is *what has been weakened and when it lapses* is
exactly where the difference belongs.

self_approved.description:
The principal that granted it also published the version.

**The filter §4.8 asks the panel for**: *show me every exemption nobody
else looked at.* A marker rather than a refusal, because four-eyes
enforced by the tool is friction a small team routes around — most often
by granting `gates:exempt` more widely, which is strictly worse.

attributes.description:
The resource attributes that apply here, composed across the tiers
(§4.1, §4.8).

§4.8 puts these on the response beside the resolved verbs, and the pair
is the point: **a caller needs both** — a grant for the verb and
membership of the audience (§4.5). A resolved set that showed
`releases:read` without saying the package is `team`-visible answers half
the question and reads as the whole one.

narrowing.description:
§4.1's compensating warnings: deeper tiers on this path that **dropped**
a constraint their parent declared.

Composition is wholesale, which is what makes a narrower policy on a
deeper tier expressible — and what makes dropping one silent. A namespace
that omits `enforce_semver` does not inherit it; it turns it off, and
nothing about the resolved answer says so. This is the edit most likely
to be a mistake in the direction that matters, so the endpoint whose job
is *why* is where it surfaces.

Empty for almost every coordinate.

not_covered.description:
What this answer does **not** account for.

The same discipline `access-check`'s `covers` field carries, and for the
same reason (RFC 0004-bis B4): a bare verdict is ambiguous between
"nothing denies this" and "nothing I looked at denies this". Grants are
the first gate, not the only one — the artifact gates, per-package
visibility and the block layers all sit behind them.

reason.description: Why, when the answer is deny.

resolved.description: Every verb this subject holds on this resource, with provenance.

oneOf.description:
Set when a node on this path is in **shadow** (§4.7), meaning a `deny`
here is *not* what the request would receive — it would be served, and
the refusal only recorded.

Reported rather than folded into `decision`, and the distinction is the
one this endpoint exists to make. Answering `allow` would hide that the
grants refuse; answering a bare `deny` would contradict what the server
actually does, and §11.6 is explicit that *"a diagnostic that can
disagree with reality is worse than none, because it is trusted."* So it
says both: the grants refuse, and the shadow serves it anyway.

tiers_walked.description:
The nodes walked, outermost first.

Includes the ones that granted nothing. A tier missing from this list is
a tier the resolver did not consider, which is a different diagnosis from
a tier that considered the subject and matched no grant.

cached_bytes.description:
Bytes held across those versions. `null` means unknown, not zero: sizes
were not recorded for artifacts cached before migration 004.

cached_versions.description: How many versions this instance currently holds bytes for.

has_blocked.description: An administrator has blocked at least one version.

has_yanked.description:
An owner has yanked at least one locally published version.

Previously reported inside `has_blocked`, which conflated an operator's
refusal with an owner's withdrawal.

last_accessed.description: When a client last downloaded this package from us (RFC 3339).

last_fetched_at.description: When this instance last fetched any version from upstream (RFC 3339).

matched_in.description:
`name` | `readme` | `both` — why this row is here.

A row whose name has nothing to do with the query and whose README
mentions it in passing is a *correct* result and an inexplicable one
without the label (RFC 0007-bis §4.3).

newest_version.description:
The version most recently obtained, by `cached_at` for a proxied
artifact or `published_at` for a local one. `null` when nothing is held.

snippet.description:
The matched fragment of the README, as **plain text**, or `null`.

Plain, and rendered as text. It never reaches `v-html`: the README
panel's is a deliberate, tested, single-component boundary
(RFC 0007 §6.5), and a search snippet is a second surface for
package-authored content reached by a much cheaper path — no navigation,
just a query (RFC 0007-bis §7.4).

state.description:
This package's standing here, in DESIGN.md's resolution vocabulary:
`"cached"` | `"stale"` | `"held"` | `"pending"` | `"yanked"` |
`"blocked"`.

Derived server-side rather than in the client because two of the six
need configuration the browser has no business holding — the registry's
artifact TTL, and the release-age gate's window and bypass roles — and
because `"held"` depends on *who is asking*.

registry.description: Registry to invalidate. When absent, the entire explore cache is cleared.

default_version.description:
The version a reader who has asked for none should be shown: the newest
stable version this instance **holds**, falling back to the newest stable
and then to whatever is held (RFC 0007 §4.2).

Answered here because it is a fact about the whole list, and the console
is now given one page of it: a client deriving this rule from the rows it
received would pick the newest stable version *on page one*, which on a
package held only at 2.1.0 is an upstream row we serve nothing of.
`None` only for a package with no versions at all.

fetch.description:
Whether the console may offer **Fetch this version** on an
upstream-only row (RFC 0007-bis §4.4).

oneOf.description:
Where this package's code and site live, as its own metadata names them.

`None` whenever we cannot say: a registry kind whose client does not read
these fields, a package the metadata cache has never held, or a locally
published one (asking a public index about a private name on a page view
would leak that the software exists — the same suppression the derived
README applies).

The selected version's row, whatever page it is on.

`selected_version` names it; this *is* it. The console renders its subject
region from this rather than from whatever happens to be in `versions`,
because the two are routinely different: the page writes `?version=X&page=N`
into the URL itself, and X is on page 1 while N is 3.

selected_version.description:
The version asked for by `version=`, echoed back **only if this package
has it**. `None` for a typo or a version yanked since the link was sent,
which is the caller's signal to fall back to `default_version` rather
than mark nothing.

upstream_unavailable.description: `true` when the upstream database was unreachable and this package has no cached data.

readme_search_enabled.description:
Whether `[search] readmes` is on for this instance.

So a client can tell "no package here says that" from "this instance does
not search prose". `in=readme` with the feature off is accepted and
answers as `in=name` does — a parameter that silently means something
else is the failure this RFC family keeps finding — and this field is how
the console says which happened (RFC 0007-bis §4.3).

searched_in.description:
The scope actually applied, which is `name` when prose search is off
however the request asked.

truncated.description:
The prose search hit [`PROSE_SEARCH_CAP`] and there may be more.

Reported rather than swallowed: a silently shortened list reads as "that
is all there is", which is a lie about the catalogue.

upstream_unavailable.description:
`true` when the upstream database was unreachable and no cached data was available.
The result set will be empty; the UI should surface a warning to the user.
`true` when the upstream database was unreachable and no cached data was available.

deprecated.description: Flagged as deprecated (still downloadable). Local versions only.

download_count.description:
`null` on an upstream-only row — **not** `0`.

`0` would be a definite answer with nothing behind it: nobody has
downloaded it *through here*, which is not the same as nobody having
downloaded it, and the row exists precisely because this instance has
never held the version (RFC 0007 §4.2).

license.description:
The licence this version's own manifest declared, verbatim.

Null means *unknown*, never "unlicensed": it is read out of the archive
when the version is cached or published, so it is absent for anything
fetched before extraction existed and for the registry types with no
manifest parser (RFC 0004-bis §13.1).

readme.description:
`available` | `none` | `unknown` — whether this version has a README.

A tri-state rather than a boolean, because the answer genuinely has three
values and the third is the common one for an archive-borne registry
kind: a version this instance holds no bytes for has a README that cannot
be read yet. `false` rendered for *"we have not looked"* would be a
definite-looking answer with nothing behind it (RFC 0007 §4.2).

sbom.description:
Which SBOM formats this version has here — the answer the console needs
*before* it draws a download control. See [`SbomDto`].

socket_badge_url.description: socket.dev badge URL when enabled for this registry; else null.

source.description:
`"proxied"` | `"local"` | `"upstream"`

`upstream` means this instance holds no bytes for the version and knows
about it only because it asked. Every cell that would be a fact about
what we hold is `null` on such a row rather than `0`.

state.description:
`cached` | `pending` | `yanked` | `blocked` — the row's state in
DESIGN.md's resolution vocabulary, graded here rather than in the
console.

The console used to derive this from `firewall` alone, over three values,
and the mapping said *held and verified* — a full 3×3 matrix in ink — for
a version this instance holds **no bytes of**: an upstream-only candidate
carries `FirewallDto::Clear`, because the firewall has nothing to refuse
about a version nobody can download from here yet. The signature device of
the whole design system was therefore lying on precisely the rows the
fetch button exists for. Grading it on the side that knows what is held
is the same correction `ExploreEntry::state` already applies to the
catalogue's rows.

Two of the six states are deliberately absent. `stale` needs the
artifact's own fetch time against the registry's TTL, and `held` needs the
release-age gate evaluated for this viewer — neither is per-version data
this endpoint holds, and inventing either would be the same class of
claim this field exists to stop.

unlisted.description:
Hidden from registry-protocol listings but still downloadable by exact
coordinate. Local versions only.

vulnerabilities.description: Known vulnerabilities for this version (from the periodic SBOM re-scan).

vulnerabilities_scanned.description:
Whether this version has ever been scanned for vulnerabilities.

`vulnerabilities: []` means *scanned and clear* only when this is `true`.
On a version nothing has ever opened it means *never scanned*, and the
two must not render identically — a green row on a package this instance
has never held is a claim we cannot support.

ExposureCoverage.description: What the report can and cannot see, printed beside its rows.

sbom_configured.description: Registries with an SBOM extractor, so the CVE scan can cover them.

security_profiles.description: Registries with a `[security]` profile, where a flag denies at once.

window_truncated_at.description:
Events older than this are gone (audit retention), so a window that
reaches past it is silently shorter than asked.

ExposureRow.description: One consumer × one coordinate × one flag.

flag_first_seen.description: When the flag was first known here.

pulls.description: Pulls in the window, and how many of them preceded the flag.

ExtensionQueryRequest.description:
`POST …/vscode/gallery/extensionquery`.

Every field is `#[serde(default)]`: a hand-written `product.json` or a
non-VS-Code client that omits half of this should get results, not a `400`.

FetchOfferDto.description:
Whether the fetch button is offered here, and why not when it is not.

Answered by the server because both halves are the server's to know: whether
the operator turned `console_fetch` off, and whether "fetch this version" has
a single meaning for this registry kind. A console that guessed would offer a
button that always fails on Maven, which is the "disabled control with no
explanation" §4.4 refuses.

reason.description:
The kind's own reason, verbatim, when `offered` is `false` and the reason
is about the registry type rather than about the switch. `null` when the
operator simply turned it off — that is not a fact about the package and
the page says nothing rather than explaining the operator to themselves.

registry.description:
The coordinate that was fetched, echoed so a client that fired several
can match responses to rows.

size_bytes.description:
What arrived, so the row can say what the wait bought.

Measured against real upstreams, the median version is 0.57 MB and the
largest in the sample was 41.7 MB (RFC 0007-bis §13.4) — a range wide
enough that "done" on its own tells a reader nothing.

Finding.description: One thing one scanner said about one artifact.

available_at.description: For a time-bound hold: when it lifts.

raw.description: The scanner's own output, untouched. Hostile data: never interpolated.

reference.description: A CVE id, an OSV id, a SOC case id — whatever the scanner cites.

FindingKind.description:
What kind of thing a finding is — the axis escalation and the console
group on.

FlagEffect.description:
How hard a flag wants the proxy to react. Ordered: `HardBlock` is the
strongest, and a source's configured ceiling caps a pushed effect down.

created.description: `false` on an update of a flag already known.

effect.description: The effect stored, after the source's ceiling was applied.

effect_capped.description: The push asked for more than the source may do.

FlagItemOutcome.description: What became of one pushed item.

oneOf.description: A published vulnerability (a CVE, a GHSA, an OSV id).
A malicious release: an install hook, a credential stealer.
A licence the estate does not accept.
An internal policy: end of life, a vendor ban.
Anything else, under the source's own name.

other.description: Anything else, under the source's own name.

FlagKind.description:
What a flag asserts. Open on purpose: a source's taxonomy is its own,
and an unknown kind is stored as it came rather than refused.

FlagPush.description: One item of a push, as the source sends it.

version.description: An exact version. Exactly one of `version` and `version_range`.

version_range.description:
Only `*` is accepted (every version); ranges wait for the
version-scheme RFC.

FlagPushBody.description:
A push: the items, and nothing else — the source is the path, the
credential the header.

FlagPushResponse.description: The answer to a push: one outcome per item, in order.

FlagSourceCoverage.description: One source's standing, for the coverage block.

git_ref.description: The ref as a client spelled it: `main`, `v2.60.0`.

previous_sha.description:
What it resolved to before, when that differs: a branch that advanced,
or a tag that moved.

ref_kind.description: `tag` or `branch`; a commit is never recorded — it cannot move.

remembered.description:
`false` when this deployment remembers no resolutions at all (no
database): the panel then says so rather than showing an empty list
that reads as "nothing moves here".

beta_member.description: Whether the caller is a beta-channel member for this registry.

GlobalBanner.description: A global administrator broadcast message shown to all website visitors.

set_by.description: user_id of the admin who set the banner, or `"system"` for auto-set messages.

GrantDto.description: One stored grant, as the API reports it.

from_ownership.description:
Whether this row is the ownership projection's rather than the editor's.

The console needs to know before it offers an edit control: these rows
are refused by `PUT` and `DELETE` (§4.3), and a UI that discovers that
from a `409` has already let the operator fill in a form.

node_key.description:
The package name, or `name@version` for a version-tier row — the same
spelling `version_node_key` stores and the CLI's positional argument
takes, so the three never have to be translated between.

Immutable.description:
Whether published bytes may be replaced — RFC 0015 §4.5.

# Why this is not a verb

**Immutability is a property of the resource, the verb is a property of the
subject, and a replace needs both.** That split is what lets a namespace be
append-only for *everyone, including admins*, which no role-based model can
say. Adding a `releases:overwrite`-style exception here would make it a rule
an admin can step over, and a rule an admin can step over is not an
invariant.

ImportFailureDto.description: One asset that did not import, named rather than counted.

repo.description:
Only run the imports whose `repo` is this one. Absent: every import
configured into the registry.

tag.description:
Import this tag instead of what the configuration selects. The only way
to reach a pre-release deliberately: `latest` will not choose one.

skipped.description:
Assets whose version this registry already holds. Not an error: it is
what makes a scheduled import free to re-run.

InboundWebhookEvent.description: A raw event received from an external system via the inbound webhook API.

signature_valid.description: `Some(true)` = HMAC verified, `Some(false)` = HMAC mismatch, `None` = no secret configured.

groups.description: Dynamic groups the user belongs to (populated by OIDC providers).

has_registry_access.description: Whether the current user has access to at least one configured registry.

MessageResponse.description:
`{"message": "…"}` — the acknowledgement the publish, yank and unyank paths
return for registries whose CLI shows the string back to the user (twine,
`gem push`, `terraform login`, `dotnet nuget push`).

The text is for a human; nothing parses it, and no client should.

MissKind.description:
What kind of thing was missing. One table, one column — the same shape
RFC 0018 uses for its single verdict table with reason codes.

air_gapped.description:
Whether this instance is actually air-gapped. A connected instance
answers with an empty list and this `false`, which is a different
fact from "nothing is missing".

empty_registries.description:
Proxy registries holding no cached artifact at all (RFC 0008 §4.5).

On an air-gapped instance such a registry answers `503` to
*everything*, and that is worth saying plainly rather than leaving an
operator to read it off an empty miss log. Empty on a connected
instance, where a registry with no cache is simply one nobody has
asked for yet.

MyAdvisoriesResponse.description: Known advisories on what the caller recently pulled and on what they own.

advisories.description:
Coordinates with findings, worst severity first. Empty means exactly
that: nothing you pulled recently or own has a known advisory.

scanning_available.description:
True when this instance records no vulnerability findings at all
(no SBOM re-scan configured). An empty list then means "we do not know",
not "you are clear" — a distinction the widget must not blur.

window_days.description:
How many days back "recently pulled" reaches, so a reader knows what
the empty case is a statement about.

MyAdvisoryDto.description: One coordinate with known advisories, and why it concerns the caller.

highest_severity.description:
The worst severity among `findings`, so a caller can rank rows without
reducing the list themselves.

MyAdvisoryFindingDto.description: One advisory finding, flattened to what a reader needs to act.

fixed_version.description: First version that fixes it, when the database reports one.

artifact.description:
The sub-artifact within the coordinate, where the registry has one
(a GitHub asset id, `tarball`, `vsix`, …).

blocked.description:
Whether this exact coordinate is blocked **now**.

The pull succeeded — this endpoint only returns successful downloads —
so this is always retroactive: something you have was refused after you
took it. That is the fact worth surfacing, and it is the miniature of
the question RFC 0002 asks at org scale ("which consumers pulled a
flagged version"), asked about yourself.

Without it the home page can list a pull it cannot describe, which is
RFC 0004 §2.2's argument reappearing on the one surface a non-admin
actually opens (RFC 0004-bis §5/A9).

MyQuotaDto.description:
One registry's quota, as it applies to the caller.

A limit of `null` means that dimension is unlimited for this registry — the
other one is what the quota measures.

oneOf.description:
This dimension's own verdict, or `null` when it has no limit. Present so
a reader can see *which* threshold was crossed (RFC 0004 §4.2) — a
registry whose versions are at 82% while its storage sits at 68% is not
"at 82%" in both.
This dimension's own verdict, or `null` when it has no limit.

state.description: The worse of the two dimensions — what the registry as a whole is at.

warn_threshold_pct.description: The percentage of a limit at which a `state` becomes `warning`.

NamespacePackageListResponse.description:
Paginated envelope for `GET /api/v1/me/namespaces/{registry}/{prefix}/packages`,
matching the shape of its sibling list endpoints (`AdminPackageListResponse`)
instead of returning a bare array with no way to tell if more pages exist.

NarrowingNote.description: One tier that dropped a constraint its parent declared (§4.1).

dropped.description: What it dropped, in the words §4.1 uses for it.

node.description: The node that dropped it, e.g. `namespace:@acme/billing`.

NotificationSubscription.description: Admin-created subscription that routes matching events to a named channel.

channel_name.description: Must match the `name` of a channel configured in `config.toml`.

event_types.description: Event types that this subscription listens for.

package_name.description: When `None`, matches all packages in the selected registries.

NpmPublishResponse.description:
npm's publish acknowledgement: an empty JSON object.

`npm publish` reports success from the status code and the quota headers;
the body carries nothing, and this type says so rather than leaving the
response undocumented.

OkResponse.description:
`{"ok": true}` — the acknowledgement several write endpoints return when the
protocol they implement expects a JSON body but has nothing to say in it.

ok.description: Always `true`; a failure is reported by the status code, not by this field.

PackageFlag.description: One assertion about a package version, from one source.

expires_at.description: After this instant the flag is dead without a revoke.

external_id.description:
The source's own id for the flag; `(source, external_id)` is the
identity a re-push updates and a revoke names.

first_seen.description:
When the source first told this proxy: the retroactive line of the
exposure report.

revoked_at.description: The tombstone: a revoked flag stays for the report and stops judging.

oneOf.description: The severity a `gate` flag is judged at; absent, `High`.

PackageId.description:
Uniquely identifies a package (or sub-artifact) in a registry.

Examples:
- GitHub release asset: `{ registry: "github", name: "rust-lang/rust", version: "v1.80.0", artifact: Some("12345678") }`
- Cargo crate:          `{ registry: "cargo",  name: "tokio",           version: "1.38.0",  artifact: None }`

PackageLinksDto.description:
A package's own links, normalised to something a browser can open.

Every URL here was written by whoever published the package and lands in an
`href` on an authenticated console page, so it has been through
`batlehub_core::entities::normalize_url` — an allow-list of `http`/`https`
applied *after* the ecosystem-specific rewrites (`git+…`, `.git`,
`github:o/r`, scp-like addresses). Anything that did not survive is absent
rather than rendered, because a link that cannot be opened is worse than no
link.

homepage.description: The package's own site, when it declared one.

PackageStatus.description: Administrative status of a package in this proxy.

PackageSummary.description: Lightweight summary used in listing endpoints.

last_accessed_by.description: User who last successfully downloaded this package. `None` means anonymous.

cached_at.description: When the artifact was first stored in the cache (null if not yet cached or pre-migration).

license.description:
The licence this version's own manifest declared, verbatim.

Null means *unknown*, never "unlicensed": the licence is read out of the
archive when it is cached or published, so it is absent for anything
fetched before extraction existed, and for the sixteen registry types
with no manifest parser. `license_gate.allow_unknown` decides how a
null is treated (RFC 0004-bis §13.1).

socket_badge_url.description:
socket.dev badge URL when the `socket_badge` feature flag is enabled for
this registry and the registry type is covered by socket.dev; else null.

storage_backend.description: Name of the storage backend holding this artifact (null if not yet cached or pre-migration).

vulnerabilities.description: Known vulnerabilities for this version (from the periodic SBOM re-scan).

PendingReloadSnapshot.description: Snapshot of a pending reload returned to the GET /pending endpoint.

warnings.description:
Warnings the *candidate* config produces (RFC 0004-bis A4).

`PendingReload` has held these since it was written — `apply()` promotes
them to the live store — and the snapshot dropped them, so the one
surface that exists to review a change before applying it could not show
what the change would warn about. The console worked around it by
remembering the warnings from the `validate` call that staged the
pending reload, which is lost on any reload of the page.

PluginPublishResponse.description:
Publish a plugin archive (local/hybrid registries only).

Accepts the marketplace upload form: `file` (the `.jar`/`.zip`), an
optional `xmlId`/`pluginId` (must match the descriptor when present),
`channel`, and `isHidden` (stored as `unlisted`: hidden from listings,
downloadable by exact coordinate).
The marketplace upload acknowledgement, in the shape the JetBrains plugin
publish API returns. `id` and `pluginId` are the same xmlId under both of
the names clients have been seen to read.

PolicyDto.description:
One node's policy, on the wire.

Every field is optional and **absent means inherit** — the same distinction
the stored row makes, carried onto the API so a client can express it. A
client that sent `visibility: "public"` where it meant "leave it alone" would
be writing an override with a default value, which stops the tier above from
applying.

rules.description:
Gate overrides, one entry per gate. Composes **per gate** (§4.1), so an
entry here replaces that gate's settings and leaves every other gate
running — sending an empty list does not disable anything, it declares no
overrides.

ProtocolDocument.description:
A non-JSON registry protocol document — `maven-metadata.xml`,
`updatePlugins.xml`, a PyPI simple-index HTML page, an APT `Release` file, a
Go `go.mod`, a plain-text token or version list.

As with [`UpstreamDocument`], the format belongs to the registry protocol.
The `Content-Type` header identifies which one.

Puller.description: One identity's pulls of one version inside the window.

identity.description:
The user id, or `ip:<addr>` for an anonymous pull, or `anonymous`
when not even the address was recorded.

PullersResponse.description: Who pulled one version (RFC 0018 §4.2 *Who pulled what*).

since.description: The start of the window the rows cover.

actions.description:
Action patterns. `releases:*` is expanded here, at write, never at
evaluation (§4.2) — the stored row carries the expanded set.

version.description: Absent addresses the package node; present, the version node.

PutGrantResponse.description: What was written, and what the operator should know about it.

actions.description:
The expanded action set actually stored, which is not always what was
asked for: `releases:*` names one thing and stores six.

warnings.description:
Legal but probably not intended — a redundant grant, a spent coordinate.
Reported rather than refused (§4.4).

QuotaStateDto.description: How close the caller is to a registry's quota.

extracted_at.description: When *this instance* read the text, not when upstream published it.

package_level.description:
The text is the package's, not this version's: npm's document-root
`readme`, attributed to the version `dist-tags.latest` names. The panel
says so rather than presenting a package-level document as this
version's.

requested_version.description: What the caller asked for, when they named a version.

stored.description:
`true` for a durable record. `false` when it was derived from a cached
upstream document for a version this instance holds no bytes for.

truncated.description: The source hit the registry's `max_bytes` and what is shown is a prefix.

version.description: The coordinate the returned text belongs to.

ReadmeState.description:
Whether a version has a README, in the three states the answer really has.

A boolean cannot carry the third one, and the third one is the common case
the moment the page starts answering for packages this instance holds nothing
of: `false` rendered for *"we have not looked"* is a definite-looking answer
with nothing behind it (RFC 0007 §4.2).

ReasonCode.description:
The closed set of reasons a verdict can carry (RFC 0018 §4.2 — this list
is the master; RFC 0019 adds its ref-level codes here).

version.description: One cached version; absent means every cached version of the name.

inconclusive.description: Packages upstream could not answer for.

missing.description: Packages (or versions of them) upstream denied.

probed.description:
Packages the probe asked upstream about: one, or zero when nothing
is cached under the name any more.

oneOf.description:
The row after the probe: absent when upstream has the package and no
miss is on record.

transitions.description:
`confirmed` or `reappeared`, one per state change the probe produced.
Empty when the row only moved to — or stayed — `missing`, or when
upstream simply has it.

RecordedMiss.description: A recorded miss, as the admin surface and the next plan read it.

count.description:
How many times it was asked for. mise retries; this is the number
that tells an operator which gap actually hurts.

held_versions.description: See [`ContentMiss::held_versions`], as of the last request.

requested_version.description:
See [`ContentMiss::requested_version`]. The last one asked for, when
the requests differed.

provider.description: Provider name that issued the refresh token. Defaults to the first configured provider.

groups.description: Group names configured with access to this registry.

roles.description: Role names (e.g. "anonymous", "user", "admin") that can access this registry.

access.description: Which roles and groups can access this registry.

beta_channel_enabled.description: Whether a beta-channel gate is configured for this registry (A2).

last_pull_at.description: Timestamp of the most recent successful download.

mode.description:
`proxy`, `local` or `hybrid` (RFC 0004-bis A2).

The health page reads "Cached artifacts: 0, last pull: never" the same
way for a broken proxy and for a healthy `local` registry that has
nothing to pull by definition. Without the mode there is no way to tell
those apart, and the console was inferring it from a second endpoint.

package_count.description: Distinct packages tracked in the DB.

pulls_last_day.description: Successful downloads in the last 24 hours.

pulls_last_hour.description: Successful downloads in the last hour.

recent_errors.description: Denied-access and upstream-error events in the last 24 h (newest first, max 10).

total_size_bytes.description: Sum of artifact sizes in bytes (null when no size data yet).

public_url.description:
The registry's own hostname-rooted URL (`https://npm.acme.io`) when one is
configured, otherwise `null` — clients then fall back to
`{origin}/proxy/{name}`.

Shown to anonymous callers too. The endpoint already filters by
`accessible_registries_for`, so a caller only ever sees registries they
can already reach; withholding the host from them would break the Setup
Guide while hiding a name that is in public DNS anyway.

signed_downloads.description:
Whether this registry mints signed download URLs (RFC 0012), and can
therefore be closed to anonymous callers even though the client fetches
artifacts without credentials.

Here so the Setup Guide can stop telling a Terraform user to open their
registry when it does not need opening. Not a secret: it changes the
advice on a page the caller can already read, and a caller who can list
a registry can discover the same fact by fetching from it.

upstream.description:
The upstream this registry proxies (`https://registry.npmjs.org`), or
`null` for a local-only registry that has none.

The design proof's catalog caption names it — *"hybrid ·
registry.npmjs.org · 1,284 packages · 6.1 GB cached"* — because "which
upstream is behind this" is the first thing an operator asks of a
registry they did not configure themselves.

Visible to anonymous callers on the same terms as `public_url` above,
and for the same reason: this endpoint already filters by
`accessible_registries_for`, so a caller only ever sees registries they
can already pull through — and pulling through one reveals the upstream
anyway, in the artifacts it returns.

RegistryScanState.description:
When the SBOM re-scan last covered a registry (RFC 0002 §4.6): a report
that cannot say when it last looked is not a report.

cached_bytes.description:
Bytes held for this registry. `null` means unknown, not zero: sizes were
not recorded for artifacts cached before migration 004.
Total bytes cached in storage for this registry (from storage backend).

hit_rate.description: Artifact hit rate in [0, 1], or null if no requests yet.

upstream_degraded.description:
`true` when upstream is showing a high error rate or slow responses;
cached data may be stale until it recovers.

upstream_error_rate.description: Rolling upstream error rate in [0, 1] (exponential moving average).

upstream_latency_ms.description: Rolling average upstream call latency in milliseconds.

RegistryStatsHistoryDto.description: One registry's series over the requested window.

pending_created.description:
Whether this call left a pending reload staged for approval.

Only `from-content` can set it: `reload` and `apply` consume the pending
rather than leave one, and `validate` is a dry run. It exists because
`from-content` returns `200` with an empty diff in two very different
situations — a pending was staged, or the submitted content was identical
to the last load attempt so there was nothing to stage. Without this flag
the caller only discovers the difference when the subsequent apply fails
with `404 No pending reload`.

warnings.description:
Non-fatal problems with the config this response describes — the one in
force for `reload`/`apply`, the candidate one for `validate`/`from-content`.
Empty for a clean config.

queued.description: `false` when an open job for the coordinate already existed.

ResolvedVerb.description: One verb, and where it came from.

kept_because.description: Why the version survived, or absent when it is to be reclaimed.

decisions.description: Per-version decisions, including the kept ones and why.

decisions_truncated.description:
How many decisions were dropped from `decisions`. Non-zero means the list
is a sample, not the answer.

incomplete_because.description:
Set when the run stopped early. `reclaimed_coordinates` is then what was
actually reclaimed before the fault, and everything after it was not
attempted — a partial run that says so, rather than an error that throws
away the record of what already happened.

reclaimed.description: Versions reclaimed, or that would be under `dry_run`.

reclaimed_coordinates.description:
The affected coordinates, `"{name}@{version}"`. The list an operator
actually reads before turning `dry_run` off.

gate.description: The gate's name, spelled as `[[registries.rules]]`'s `kind` tag does.

settings.description: The gate's settings, in the same shape the config block uses.

SbomDocument.description:
An SPDX 2.3 or CycloneDX 1.5 document.

The shape is the SBOM standard's, not this API's — which format you get is
decided by the `format` query parameter, and each is specified elsewhere.

SbomDto.description:
Which SBOM formats a version actually has here, so the console can say *no
SBOM* instead of offering a download that can only 404.

The formats are per registry (`[registries.sbom].formats`), so a console that
assumed both drew a CycloneDX button on an SPDX-only registry and a pair of
them on every upstream-only row — three clicks, three spinners, three
failures, and the reader left to guess whether the SBOM was missing or the
server was.

A tri-state for the same reason [`ReadmeState`] is one: *we hold none* and
*we have not looked* are different answers, and rendering the second as the
first is a definite claim with nothing behind it (RFC 0007 §4.2).

formats.description:
The formats actually held, `"spdx"` before `"cyclonedx"`. Empty unless
`state` is `available`.

SetExemptionRequest.description:
The request body for setting an exemption.

`exempt_until` and `reason` are **required by the type**, not merely
validated — the same discipline §4.7 gives `grants.dry_run`, because the
realistic failure is not a wrong assessment but a right assessment nobody
revisited.

Severity.description:
Severity bucket for a vulnerability finding, ordered from least to most severe.

`Ord` is derived from declaration order, so `Critical > High > Medium > Low > Unknown`.
This lets the CVE gate compare a finding's severity against a configured minimum
with a plain `>=`.

ShadowNote.description: A node whose shadow is currently serving what its grants refuse.

by_node.description:
Per node, busiest first — an operator triaging a migration reads
top-down.

kept.description:
How many entries the buffer keeps at most.

Reported rather than assumed, because `recent.len() == kept` is the one
state where an operator must not read the list as complete — a bounded
buffer that looked exhaustive would understate what a shadow is serving,
which is the wrong direction for this page.

no_shadow_configured.description:
`true` when nothing is being shadowed at all — no node in the loaded
config carries a `grants_shadow` block.

Distinguishes "the shadow is quiet" from "there is no shadow", which look
identical in an empty list and mean opposite things: the first says
enforcing is safe, the second says nothing was measured.

ShadowSummaryDto.description:
One node's shadow, summarised.

The shape the question actually has. *"Can I enforce this namespace yet?"* is
answered by which verbs are still missing and for whom, not by a list of
requests — and a busy registry produces thousands of the latter for a handful
of the former.

actions.description: The distinct verbs that were missing, in the order first seen.

count.description: How many requests this node's shadow has served.

subjects.description: The distinct subjects that lacked them.

ShadowedDenialDto.description: One request shadow mode served that enforcement would have refused.

action.description: The verb the caller did not hold.

node.description: The node whose shadow served the request.

subject.description:
The subject, in the spelling a grant would be written in — so it can be
pasted into the block that would fix this.

SigningKeyDto.description: One key, in Terraform's own field names.

key_id.description: The long key id, uppercase hex without `0x`.

SimulationCoverage.description:
Which enforcement layers the answer actually accounts for.

The simulator used to evaluate `policy.rules` and nothing else, so an admin
who blocked `alice` on `/admin/security/blocks` and simulated `alice` on the
next tab was told **allow** — the page whose entire purpose is "would this
identity be allowed" contradicted by the section it lives in.

Stating coverage is part of the fix rather than a nicety: two of the three
layers are only checkable when the caller supplies the input they key on, so
a bare `allow` is ambiguous between "nothing denies this" and "nothing I
looked at denies this".

account_blocks.description: True when `user_id` was supplied, so the account block list was consulted.

ip_blocks.description: True when `client_ip` was supplied, so the IP block list was consulted.

rules.description: Always true — the registry's rule chain is evaluated in full.

StatsHistoryPointDto.description: One hour of one registry's cache activity.

cached_bytes.description: Bytes in storage at the end of the window. A level, not a delta.

hits.description:
Hits **in this window**, not a running total — which is the whole point
of the table: a counter since process start cannot survive a deploy.

per_registry.description:
Per registry, oldest point first. Registries with no rows in the window
are absent rather than present-and-empty.

window_days.description: The window actually used, after clamping.

since_startup.description: When this process started (counters reset on restart).

StatsTrendDto.description:
The dashboard's trend: this window against the one before it.

Both halves are computed server-side so the two numbers being compared are
always derived the same way. A client differencing two separate requests
would be one off-by-one away from comparing 30 days with 29.

delta.description:
`hit_rate - previous_hit_rate`, or `null` when either side is unknown.
Present so a reader is not left subtracting two nullable numbers.

hit_rate.description:
Hit rate in [0, 1] for the requested window, or `null` when it saw no
traffic at all — which is not the same as a hit rate of zero.

previous_hit_rate.description:
The same rate over the equally-long window immediately before it, or
`null` when there is no history that far back yet.

sources.description:
Where it was seen. A subject seen in more than one place lists all of
them, so an operator can tell a namespace owner who has never pulled
anything from an account that is only in the audit log.

user_id.description: The identity as this instance stores it — `oidc:alice`, not `alice`.

truncated.description:
True when the limit truncated the answer, so a field can say "keep
typing" rather than implying it has shown everything.

package_count.description:
How many packages the namespace currently holds (RFC 0004-bis A6).

`count_packages_in_namespace` has been on `TeamNamespacePort` since the
port was written and had exactly one caller — the *delete* confirmation.
The list showed a row per claim with no way to tell a namespace holding
four hundred packages from an abandoned one, which is the question an
operator opens this page with.

groups.description:
The groups this token resolves to. Listed because a snapshot goes stale
silently: nothing tells its owner that the token still carries a team
they left, and this column is where they can see it.

last_used_at.description:
When this token was last presented, or `null` if not since the server
started recording. What tells a user which of their tokens is dormant and
safe to revoke, and an operator which one moved after a leak.

TombstoneDto.description:
One deleted coordinate.

Mirrors [`Tombstone`] rather than re-exporting it, so the API shape is a
decision this crate makes: the entity is what the store holds, and the two
are free to diverge when the store gains a column the API should not carry.

deleted_by.description: The identity that deleted it, when the deletion carried one.

detail_compacted_at.description:
RFC 3339 timestamp of when this tombstone's detail was stripped, or
absent when it still has it. The field that tells a reader whether an
absent `checksum` means "never recorded" or "aged out".

published_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of the original publish. Never stripped.

UpstreamDocument.description:
A JSON document produced by the registry protocol rather than by this
server's own API.

In `proxy` mode it is the upstream's response forwarded (with URLs rewritten
where the protocol requires it); in `local` mode this server generates the
same protocol document. Either way the shape is the registry protocol's to
define, not this API's — npm's packument, NuGet's registration index and
Composer's `packages.json` are each specified by their own ecosystem, and
this server does not narrow them.

Documented as an unconstrained JSON value rather than an object: several of
these protocols answer with a top-level array, and a client that trusted a
fabricated object schema would be wrong about half of them. Where the shape
*is* known to be a list, the endpoint declares `Vec<UpstreamDocument>`.

already_cached.description: `true` when this package already exists in the proxy cache or local registry.

fetch.description:
Whether the catalogue may offer **Fetch** on this row (RFC 0007-bis
§11 q3).

Per row rather than per response: a listing with no registry filter fans
out across every registry the caller may browse, and `console_fetch` and
the kind's own answer are both per registry — so one flag for the page
would be wrong for some of its rows.

UpstreamPackageStatus.description:
What the audit knows about one package: its rows, whole-package and
per-version (RFC 0014 §4.6).

rows.description: Empty when upstream has it and no miss is on record.

UpstreamReadDto.description:
What the discovery read did, so the page can say which rung answered rather
than presenting a degraded answer as a complete one.

attempted.description:
`false` for a `local`-mode registry, a kind with no upstream to ask, a
`?upstream=skip` caller, a registry with the read disabled, or a package
published here — a private name is never sent to a public index.

error.description:
Set when the read was attempted and every rung failed. The page says the
upstream could not be reached rather than showing an empty table as an
answer.

truncated.description:
`max_versions` shortened the list. A silently shortened list is a lie
about the registry.

version_count.description: How many upstream-only versions came back.

overridden.description: Whether `policy` is the registry's own row rather than the estate's key.

policy.description:
The policy that applies to this registry (RFC 0014 §13 O6): its own
`on_confirmed` row when it has one, else the page's `policy`.

last_error.description: The upstream error as last seen, for the console. Never parsed.

version.description: `None` = the whole package is gone, not one version.

counts.description:
Per audited registry, how many rows are `missing` and how many
`disappeared` — the health card's numbers, unfiltered.

policy.description:
`audit` or `block`: what a confirmation does on this instance. On the
listing so a console never has to answer "check the config file".

total.description: Rows matching the filter, every page included.

UpstreamStatusSummary.description:
One `upstream_status` row, as the console shows it (RFC 0014 §4.6
`UpstreamStatusSummary`).

last_error.description: The upstream's last error, verbatim and bounded; never parsed.

version.description: Absent for a whole-package row: every cached version went at once.

Verdict.description: The persisted decision about one version (RFC 0018 §6.1).

available_at.description: When a time-bound hold lifts, if this verdict is one.

scanners_done.description:
The scanners that have answered for this version, so "pending" is
derived rather than guessed on every read.

VerdictListResponse.description:
The admin listing: the verdicts of one registry, newest evaluation
first, per state (RFC 0018 §4.2 *CLI*: `batlehub verdicts list`).

findings_withheld.description:
Whether `findings` was withheld for lack of `findings:read`, so a
client can tell "no findings" from "not allowed to see them".

requested_ref.description:
RFC 0019 phase 2 — on a forge, what the ref in the request resolved
to. `batlehub why github:cli/cli@main` asks about a branch; the
verdict is keyed on the commit, and these three fields are how the
answer says which one.

VerdictResponse.description:
A verdict as the endpoint serves it: the stored row, findings only for a
caller with `findings:read`.

VerdictState.description: What the proxy does with an artifact under this verdict.

VersionPageDto.description:
Where the returned rows sit in the whole version list.

Every count here is over the *whole* list rather than the page, because each
one answers a question the console asks out loud — `42 of 44 shown`, `Show 3
pre-releases`, how many pages there are — and a count taken from the page
would make each of those sentences false as soon as there was more than one.

hidden_prereleases.description:
How many the pre-release mode is currently removing. Not the same number
as `prerelease_total`: `version=` keeps its own, so a page opened on a
release candidate hides one fewer than it has.

page.description:
0-based, and the page **actually returned**: the one holding `version=`
when the caller named one and asked for no page, or the last page when
the ask was past the end.

per_page.description:
The page size actually applied, after the `[limits].versions_per_page`
ceiling. A caller that asked for more gets this, not what it asked for.

prerelease_total.description:
Pre-releases this package has, whatever the mode — the number behind
*Show 3 pre-releases*.

total.description: Versions matching `q` and the pre-release mode, across every page.

unfiltered_total.description: Versions this endpoint knows of, before either filter.

Visibility.description:
How wide the audience for a resource is — RFC 0015 §4.5's one *narrowing*
dimension.

Grants and visibility answer the same question from opposite directions, and
the model ships both deliberately: a grant says *this subject may* and
composes by union, so it can only ever widen; visibility says *the audience
is this wide*, is a single scalar, and composes deepest-wins, so it can only
ever narrow. **A caller needs both** — a grant for the verb and membership of
the audience — which is an AND, not a fallback. A `releases:read` grant does
not make a `team` package public, and a `public` namespace does not serve a
caller no grant matches.

The variants are declared widest to narrowest. Nothing in production compares
two of them today — visibility composes deepest-wins, which picks a value
rather than ordering two — but the derived `Ord` is part of the type's public
shape, and an enum whose order reads as arbitrary is one somebody reorders for
readability. `visibility_is_ordered_widest_to_narrowest` pins it.

visibility.description:
The three-valued enum, not a free string: the console narrowed this by
hand until RFC 0004, and a narrowing the client invents is one the
server can break without noticing.

VulnerabilityDto.description:
A known vulnerability affecting a package version, surfaced from the periodic
SBOM re-scan. Shared by the admin and explore package-detail views.

WarmFailureDto.description: One package or path that did not warm (RFC 0004-bis A3).

package.description: Package name, or the upstream path for a path-addressed registry.

version.description: The version that failed. Absent when listing the versions is what failed.

package.description:
A package name to warm, optionally with a pinned version (`"lodash"` or
`"lodash@4.17.21"`). Use for package-centric registries.

packages.description: Multiple package names to warm (same form as `package`).

path.description:
A single upstream artifact path to warm, for path-addressed registries
(`deb`/`rpm`/`jetbrains`), e.g. `"idea/idea-2026.1.3.tar.gz"`.

paths.description: Multiple upstream artifact paths to warm (same form as `path`).

versions.description:
Override the number of most-recent versions to warm per package. Falls back
to the registry's `warm_latest_n` config when absent.

failures.description:
One entry per named failure, as the bulk endpoints already return.

`errors` remains the count: a warming task that panics is counted here
and cannot be named, so `failures.len() <= errors`. Reporting only the
count left an operator with "3 errors" over eleven registries and no way
to learn which three without reading the server log.
